utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- cross-examine the witness. Mr. Stewart, I do understand that there are a few technical matters in relation to the transcript that you'd like to draw the Chamber's attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, I think you should try to find a witness and I'll apologise for a second if he comes in. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This will be very brief, Your Honour. With the Court's permission, I reviewed the transcript, the LiveNote transcript, and confirmed that there are two errors in the official transcript. If I can direct the Court's attention to the two errors. I've discussed both errors with Mr. Stewart, and he's prepared to enter into a stipulation as to the corrections that I'm going to propose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The first appears on page 13030 at line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What day is that, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the -- the error is the acronym UNTSO. I then said the United Nations Truce Supervision Organisation. What is in the record is "truth," instead of "truce."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Stewart will accept that that correction should be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: T-r-u-c-e rather than T-r-u-t-h.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The second error appears on page 13054 of yesterday's transcript, line 16, in that General Wilson was describing the types of heavy weapons that were available to the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And it describes mortars of 160 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And it should be 120 millimetre. And Mr. Stewart - - I've raised that issue with Mr. Stewart and he accepts that correction as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is, then, on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Wilson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Defence counsel will now have an opportunity to cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Wilson, my apologies to those on the Internet in Australia for depriving them of an opportunity of an all Australian tussle by not having my co-counsel cross-examine you. You'll have to make do with me, Mr. Wilson. First of all, I would just like to clear up a couple of smallish points about your own movements during the period in question. The -- in the -- your final report after your tour of duty, which was P720. That's a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If the witness might have that. That was his report dated the 15th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've set out on the second page under -- it's paragraph 4, "Outline of movements," which is what it says. And then you've set out your own movements. I just want to confirm with you: Under item, letter (I), 29th of April to 9th of May, CMO, that's you, returns to UNTSO. So that was -- that was where?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That was returning from -- sorry, wrong. I had left Sarajevo on or about the 29th and returned to Jerusalem to pack up my wife and send her back to Australia. She'd been left in Jerusalem while I'd been temporarily deployed to Yugoslavia in January and February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I wanted to clarify. So the where was to Jerusalem. And then I think you must have come back from -- from the looks of this, you must have come back from Jerusalem on about the 9th of May. And then -- then you -- you returned to Belgrade and then made your way from Belgrade back to Sarajevo. Is -- is that right? Because on the -- I'm going from the transcript yesterday where you said - this is page 24 of that version of the transcript - where you said that you had travelled on the 13th of May, you travelled from Belgrade to Sarajevo. So you went from Jerusalem to Belgrade for a few days, did you, and then down to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And, in fact, it was the 13th of May that I relocated. I have good reasons for remembering that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then as it appears from your report, then, you got back to Sarajevo on the 13th. UNPROFOR itself, as an organisation, it relocated to Belgrade but you stayed in Sarajevo, as you've indicated, but just until the 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: 25th or 24th. I think this is slightly different to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we're --

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: -- my statement. What was in my statement says the 24th. This says the 25th. About the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Wilson, if neither you nor the Trial Chamber are worried about that one day, neither am I. So the -- thank you very much for that. So the -- but the picture we have, then, is that, as you described in your evidence yesterday, for the first few months of your tour of duty the focus of your work was more towards Croatia than Bosnia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It was almost exclusively towards Croatia until about the 22nd of March, when UNPROFOR deployed to Bosnia-Herzegovina and I accompanied that deployment, and I then had to be concerned about the deployment of the military observers to the two designated areas, which, as I said yesterday, was UNPROFOR's only operational interest in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were on a -- whatever the steepness of the learning curve that you found yourself on, it's not unfair to say that you, as far as -- as Bosnia and Herzegovina was concerned, you were in January/February 1992, you were very far down towards the bottom of the curve in relation to Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It's true to say in January/February I knew very little about Bosnia-Herzegovina, although my -- my knowledge grew the longer I stayed in the former Yugoslavia. And certainly by March I was beginning to develop a -- an understanding of the -- the geography and events that were emerging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you said - and this was page 10 of yesterday's evidence - you said that it had been pointed out to you that should the conflict spread from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina, it would be far more serious, have much more impact than had been the case in Croatia, and you said this surprised you at the time because you were unaware there was any likelihood of the conflict spreading. Those conversations - and I think you indicated that some of this information came from the Croat politicians, among others - but that was -- the time period there is early 1992, is it, January/February 1992 that you were hearing these things?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: January/February. More likely February. But it was not from Croat politicians, it was Croat military that I heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Now, in your -- this same report that is in front of you, you indicated that paragraph 6 was really concerned with Croatia and then paragraph 7 in terms indicates, of course, that you're turning to Bosnia in -- in this report. The -- you described -- Mr. Harmon asked you questions about the -- the basis of your information here, and you said that it was - - he said: "Was this based on your personal observations, your contacts with leaders from the respective parties, based on reports that you'd received from responsible third parties? What was it based on?" And then you said, "All those elements." And then you said, "My observations from almost 12 months in UNPROFOR, my personal contacts with the political leadership at the highest level." Now, when you're -- when you're talking about the 12 months with UNPROFOR up to November 1992, that answer relates to not just Bosnia but to Croatia and, of course, aspects of Serbia's involvement and Bosnia and Herzegovina. So you're talking -- the personal contacts with political leadership is all over that area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and it also includes President Tudjman and President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so far as your personal contacts with Mr. Krajisnik are concerned, we can -- can we narrow it down to this, that first of all you say that you came into contact with him just on one day of the Sarajevo airport negotiations? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then came into contact with him, as you've described, on a number of occasions where you and he were both present in your different capacities at the international conference, at meetings in early -- well, the first half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that you also did meet Mr. Krajisnik on an occasion when you went to Pale and Mr. -- General Panic was also present on that occasion? Do you have any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I don't. My recollection is that I met General Panic in Lukavica and that he also came to the PTT building and that I transported him to the Marsal Tito Barracks and left him there overnight and picked him up again the next morning. I have no recollection of going to Pale, in fact, at any time for a meeting; although, I do acknowledge that during 1993 I certainly -- wrong. Probably later in 1992 I visited some of the Serb gun positions in the area of Pale that my observers were manning. So in short, I -- I don't recall ever having a meeting in Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there may be no big issue here, Mr. Wilson. If -- if Mr. Krajisnik -- if Mr. Krajisnik should say that he -- he did on one occasion meet you to whatever extent in Pale, you're not saying it wasn't so, are you? You're just saying you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm saying I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But so we therefore have, if we do, for the sake of today's purposes, we'd add such a meeting to the list. We're talking about three categories of meeting; one of them the single meeting, airport negotiations; the second category, as we've said, the international conference; the third category, again, the single meeting, if Mr. Krajisnik is right, in Pale. And that's it. There's no other occasion that you say you ever met Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No. But I -- I did meet him while I was in the same area, in the same room with him on many occasions in my role at ICFY, and not always in Geneva, but on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mm-hm. You -- you never actually sat down -- well, it doesn't matter whether you sat down. You never actually had a conversation yourself with Mr. Krajisnik, did you, Mr. Wilson?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I can't recall that I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you had had a conversation, it would have had to be through an interpreter because I take it you -- you did not at the time anyway - whether you do now - you did not speak Mr. Krajisnik's language.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, and nor to my knowledge did he speak English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are correct about that, Mr. Wilson, just to make that clear to you. The -- the airport negotiations that you've described, then, the last day that you say that Mr. Krajisnik came to those discussions/negotiations, was that the same day that you recall an agreement being signed? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present at any actual signing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I believe I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you observe signed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I believe it was Dr. Karadzic signed on behalf of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that final day -- and it was just that one day, according to you, that Mr. Krajisnik was present - and I'm not challenging that there was no other occasion, Mr. Wilson - on that last day, was there anything significant which remained to be negotiated and resolved before the signing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you'll have to rephrase that question. I mean, there -- there were many items of detail that had to be sorted out by General MacKenzie and Lieutenant Colonel Gray in terms of the implementation of the plans. If you're talking about were there any further matters unrelated to the plan, I'm not quite sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will rephrase it, then. I'll put it in a completely different way, Mr. Wilson. On that day that you say Mr. Krajisnik was added to the group and the same day -- that being the same day that the agreement was signed, was there anything of significance remaining to be negotiated on that day and resolved, as opposed to the signing of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, the proposal in regard to Sarajevo at that time was that it be demilitarised, and it was to happen, as I understood it, in two phases: Phase one was the opening of the airport; phase two was the withdrawal of heavy weapons out of range of the airport. Mr. Thornbury came -- came down to Sarajevo with a brief that we would concentrate on phase one and phase two, the demilitarisation of Sarajevo, would be addressed at a later date. The Bosnian Serb president from the Bosnian Presidency was very keen to negotiate stage two at that time. So it was certainly a matter that was yet to be resolved, even after the signing of the airport deal. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the day that you've described that Mr. Krajisnik came and the agreement was signed, did you and as far as you're aware other people present at that meeting, turn up that day in the clear expectation that there was going to be a signing because for practical purposes they got agreement on that phase of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Actually, we were quite pessimistic when we turned up on that day. The Serb side had been quite inflexible in the previous few days of negotiation, and it was only on the evening before the last day when they realised that it was not possible for them to retain practical control of the airport, that they indicated that they might be prepared to in fact hand over the airport, as had originally indicated. So when Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik were present on the last day, we took that as a very positive sign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the process you've just described, you -- you were pessimistic but at some point on the evening before this -- this day you received some indications that the Serb position was becoming more cooperative.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that -- to just slightly reput the question: On the actual day, having had that indication the evening before -- on the actual day, you were turning up with a -- an expectation there was going to be a signing that day.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no. As I said, there was an indication of greater flexibility on the evening before, but these things come and go in negotiations in that part of the world. We really thought that on the 5th of June that if -- if we couldn't get a - an agreement on that day, it was all over and we would have to try at a later time. And as I indicated, when we saw the expanded leadership there, we were then -- we then realised after we had arrived that maybe we had a chance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything that was actually in dispute on that last day and still the subject of active disagreement and negotiation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two phases or two stages, if you like, were these, weren't they: That, first of all, the airport -- the agreement was reached that the airport should be opened for humanitarian aid; and then the second stage, that the airport was turned over to United Nations control?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's not my understanding. My understanding was -- well, perhaps there's some semantics here. But our --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explain it the way you -- you recall it, Mr. Wilson, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: My understanding, that the offer was that the airport would be handed over to the United Nations so that humanitarian aid can flow. And secondly, when that had been achieved, there would be negotiations about the demilitarisation and the withdrawal of heavy weapons from around the Sarajevo area. I can't envisage that -- that we would have negotiated on the basis that humanitarian supplies would have gone through the airport and been controlled and delivered by the Serbs. It would not have been practical. I'd had numerous discussions with Mrs. Plavsic about the possibility of road transport running humanitarian supplies into the city. She and General Mladic had said this was logistically very difficult because of the many different areas the transport would have to transit before it got to Sarajevo. My recollection is that the proposal was the UN would have the airport. It was the Serb position that they would retain control of the airport, and this was unacceptable to the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you -- you said a few moments ago -- I asked you whether you could recall anything actually in dispute on that last day and still the subject of active disagreement and negotiation, and you very fairly said you couldn't. You had also given evidence - and this was at page 37 of yesterday's transcript - that on that last day Dr. Karadzic had at some -- had at some point taken General Mladic out of the room, evidently to the room next door, and one could hear a violent argument between the two of them, and then when they came back into the room, Dr. Karadzic announced that the Serb side was prepared to accept the agreement. Mladic no longer raised any objections to it. Now, the first question is: It appears to follow, but can you confirm, then, that you -- you don't actually -- you don't actually know the specific content of that argument that you overheard between Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, it was conducted in their language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was in some way obvious to you, was it, that General Mladic was saying "no" to the signing of the agreement, was it, and that Dr. Karadzic was saying "yes"? Was it -- was it as simple as that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Throughout the whole negotiations, General Mladic had said no, he couldn't hand over the airport. Serb forces had fought for it, lives had been lost, and he wouldn't be able to convince his soldiers that they should give up this hard-won territory. I think he continued that position until this argument that I've related to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's -- so that's the -- that's the most you can tell us about that argument, its content, what it was about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Indeed. I mean, during the negotiations, as I'd indicated yesterday, the Serb position was to retain control of the airport while there would be a -- a pseudo-presence of the UN, but in practical terms the Serbs would retain the military advantage of holding that ground and operating the airport. And they'd made many proposals, which on the surface could appear to be quite innocent, but clearly though intended to give them some sort of foot in the door to be able to maintain control. Mr. Thornbury and I were quite insistent that the UN had to wholly control that airport and the access to the airport, but there would be concessions to both parties to make sure that the airport was used for that purpose and that purpose alone and that the Muslims would not be able to exploit in a military sense the fact that the Serbs had given up this territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described in your evidence - same page yesterday, page 37 - how on a number of occasions from late May and through the airport negotiations you had asked General Mladic whether he was subordinate to and responsible and that -- and you said and responsive to the political leadership. The -- when you asked him, you're talking, are you, about asking him in the course of these meetings either in the actual meeting or just outside the meeting during a break; is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: In both those situations. This had become almost a joke between General Mladic and I because the frequency that I'd raised it during -- during May. I guess the thing that promoted these series of discussions was Colonel Kadja [phoen] having wronged the Bosnians -- the Bosnian Presidency brought an audiotape of General Mladic directing artillery fire against Sarajevo, and they played it at one of the negotiating sessions for the evacuation of the barracks. Colonel Kadja identified the voice as that of General Mladic and indicated that General Mladic was out of control and doing his own -- his own thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is this right, that the -- when you raised this issue with General Mladic, it was raised in the context that you knew and he knew that there were these concerns being expressed by JNA representatives that he, General Mladic, was in some way out of control, acting independently and irrationally? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know what General Mladic knew about the attitude of the JNA. I was not privy to -- to his knowledge or concerns in that regard. I -- I simply raised them because there was this concern that maybe this man was unstable and he was acting in -- in such a -- an erratic way or that the conduct of the operation was being done in such a brutal way, such an indiscriminate way. I was trying to get some sort of idea who was actually running this operation against Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's just that whatever -- whatever degree of -- or whatever note of jocularity you managed to inject between you two senior military men in the course of your discussions, the serious point must have been, Mr. Wilson, when you raised this issue with General Mladic that he was in some way acting out of control.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I indicated to him that what he was doing was in contravention of the Geneva Conventions at least once, if not more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when he made it clear to you on -- these are your words in your evidence yesterday. When he made it clear to you on a number of occasions that he was responsible or responsive to his political leadership, his assurances given to you were given in response to what must have been understood as a -- some form of quite serious accusation about his conduct.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you -- you said in your evidence in relation to this same topic - this is at the foot of page 42 yesterday - you said: "General Mladic is a very strong personality," Mr. Wilson. That's not, I think, going to be one of the issues in dispute in this case. "General Mladic was a strong personality, a very strong personality, but nevertheless," you said -- the bottom line is, "He did what his political masters told him to do." Now, you've given the Trial Chamber a description of that particular incident on the last day of the airport negotiations, the violent disagreement between Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic. Otherwise, do you have yourself any firsthand knowledge of that bottom line operating and doing what General Mladic doing what his political masters told him to do?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, I think the -- the airport negotiations are a very stark example of a military leader who would consistently, over a number of days, hold a position which was contrary to that of the political participants in the negotiations, suddenly changing his mind and -- and adhering to his political masters. Other than that, one has to say that the operations of the Bosnian Serb army conducted over a wide area were -- were quite a sophisticated military set-up, well organised, required good command and control, communications, direction. All of this was no accident. This was a -- quite a professional military that was getting on with the job that they had to do. And it appeared to be directed at achieving the political aims that were quite clearly stated; that is, setting up separate Serb territory. It's no accident that the military operations seemed to mirror requirements of the political ambitions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Wilson, that's an expression of view by you on what we might call the -- the big issues in this case. My -- and ultimately there's big issues really before the Trial Chamber to be resolved over a period of about two years. But the specific question -- let's leave aside the airport agreement and airport negotiations now. Do you have any firsthand knowledge of that bottom line coming into operation and General Mladic being told by his political masters, "You do this, Mladic"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, there's the -- the barracks negotiations. Once again, General Mladic's position on this was that there was to be no handover of weapons. In the end, somebody told him that -- that there would be a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. handover of weapons. In fact, two semitrailer loads of small arms were handed over on the road outside the PTT. It was part of the deal for the evacuation of the Marsal Tito Barracks. Now, whether it was the JNA, in the form of General Panic, or whether it was the Bosnian Serb political leadership, I can't say. But here is another case of a man who dramatically changed his position, and he'd expressed violent opposition to a particular proposal. There are also numerous times where relatively small humanitarian activities were negotiated by Mrs. Plavsic and implemented with the assistance, or at least the tolerance, of the Serb military. I presume there'd been some communication between Mrs. Plavsic and General Mladic on these matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talk about the international conference meetings at which you were an observer, as you've described, you said - and this is page 47 of yesterday's transcript - you said, "Mr. Krajisnik didn't have a lot to say." You assume this is because he didn't speak English. You say, "Certainly he was very carefully consulted by Dr. Karadzic," -- by Mr. Karadzic or Dr. Karadzic. "He sat at a central part of the table and he seemed to be a very important member of the delegation." Now, Mr. Wilson, you -- I take it you obviously knew what actual official positions the various people concerned held at the time when they attended these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: By then I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, but you say "by then." When did you -- did you -- did you know at the time of the airport negotiations precisely what Mr. Krajisnik's official position was in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I didn't. The Republic -- Serb Republic was a new entity to me, at least at that time. I can never recall having met Mr. Krajisnik before that. I don't know that his -- his title was introduced at that meeting. It was evident to me that he was simply a very important member of the team who had been brought in to help make a decision on the airport. I got to know his appointment later in UNPROFOR, probably saw it in various pieces of paper. But I -- I don't recall, again, meeting Mr. Krajisnik until Geneva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you got to know -- after the airport negotiations you got to know of his appointment, what, then, did you learn was his appointment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I understood he was the speaker of the Serb Parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he attended the international conference meetings, was your understanding the same, that he -- he was -- well, he was there as a member of the negotiating team, of course, but that the -- behind that, the basis of his attendance was that he was speaker of the Republika Srpska Assembly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that he retained that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an observer at that international conference, was it -- did you have some knowledge and understanding of what would have to happen to any agreement that was accepted by the Bosnian Serb leadership when they went home?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Are you talking about selling it politically to the population, or are you talking about military implementation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's take just the first and then see whether it's necessary to go to the second. So yes, talking about political implementation.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, clearly politicians on all sides would have had to sell the settlement to their respective populations. Yes, I understand -- understood that the delegation would have to sell it to their own population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Harmon, any need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I just have one moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have no additional questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Wilson, I would have a few questions for you in relation to your testimony of yesterday. Let me first try to find the exact words. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked whether at the negotiations where Lord Owen was in charge, whether there were any claims expressed of ethnic cleansing committed by the Serbs in Bosnia, and your answer said -- in your answer, you said, "Yes, there were." And then you explained how Lord Owen on occasions when negotiations were not progressing smoothly would sometimes lecture the participants on their conduct and on their failure to respect human rights. Ethnic cleansing and violation of human rights is, of course, not the same. How should I understand your answer that -- should I understand you yes, to be that specifically ethnic cleansing was then mentioned, or should I understand your answer to be that Lord Owen was mainly lecturing them on violation of human rights in more general terms? I would like to add to that question: You said that he was rather blunt in his expression. Perhaps you could give an example -- well, could you please answer my question and perhaps if you could illustrate it by some of the language as used by Lord Owen. I would highly appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Lord Owen spoke about both ethnic cleansing and human rights. He was talking about things like prisoner of war camps or detention centres. He was talking about the physical process of ethnic cleansing of areas. He was talking about military operations conducted against civilian populations. He was covering the broad gambit of activities, not only by the Serbs but also certainly by the Croats and to a lesser extent by Presidency forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't recall a particular sentence, but I mean, there was absolutely no doubt. You know, he was talking in the most direct language, that you people are doing this and you're going to be held accountable for it, that you're clearing out these areas, you are murdering people. These were -- it's the sort of words. He was not using abusive language, per se, but certainly very direct language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: More so where -- Mr. Eagleburger who I think was a former US Secretary of State at a plenary -- at a central session. Once again, he spoke in the most direct terms to all of the parties about the nature of their activities in the former Yugoslavia. And he also said that they would be held accountable. And that was certainly translated to everybody present. There's no doubt in my mind that the leaders of all of the delegations who attended, ICFY, were well aware of the co-chairman's position and the international community's position on the conduct of operations down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that include, just to say it as clearly, would that include specific reference to driving out civilian population from the area where they lived?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I take it civilian population of the other ethnicity, since you were talking about Croats and Bosnian Serbs and to a lesser extent Muslims, but that would mean Serbs against non-Serbs, Croats against non-Croats, I take it, Muslims against non-Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes. Although, I -- to be honest, I think the -- the Muslim activities were probably more directed in military areas of their control. Whether it was ethnically motivated, I don't know. But clearly on the Croat and Serb side there were ethnic issued involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were asked yesterday about the positions the Serbs took in respect of living -- the ability to live with non-Serbs. And then you said that they indicated that it was no longer possible for the three nations to continue to live together in harmony in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was necessary to physically and politically separate the nations. What did you mean exactly by "physically separate the nations"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: My understanding of their position was that they needed a separate political entity, a separate republic, that they were not interested in the sharing of power with other nationalities to run that republic, and that the -- the territory of that republic should be ethnically pure Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does this understanding include, in terms of physical separation, that where the areas would be of mixed ethnicity that the non-Serb population could not remain there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour. During the negotiations in Geneva, territories which were under Serb control but which still had other nationalities residing in them, during negotiations these were identified, and it was generally agreed by all of the parties, all three parties, that if necessary those non-Serb people or, depending on the territory, would be relocated, physically relocated as part of the settlement. It seemed to be an accepted norm by the three parties that in -- if it had to be a division and it did involve the physical removal of people who were still residing there in 1993, then that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. This brings me to my next question, but again in order not to misquote you, I'd rather find the literal text. You suggested, "There was never any really denial of facts on the ground that areas had -- that longer," and I understood that to be no longer, "had their original population, that there had been already in the process of the war ethnic cleansing or relocation of population." You said "ethnic cleansing or relocation." What exactly is the difference for you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There is no difference. Just a redundancy in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that mean that the relocation you are talking about at that moment, which you now say was equal to ethnic cleansing, was done by force? Is that an element of ethnic cleansing for you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I was really referring to ethnic cleansing. There was no need for me to use the words "or relocation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now but --

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Simply redundant words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But does that include force or threat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: "Ethnic cleansing" does -- does in my definition--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: -- include force or the threat of force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have one or two questions also on the negotiations on the airport agreement. You were asked whether there was anything left to negotiate after that day when you at least saw some optimism. I'll try to carefully understand what you've said, and if I'm not mistaken, you said that at the evening before they said that they might give up - which they had refused until that moment - the control over the airport. You also said that the next day there was not much to negotiate anymore or -- but was it then already clear that they would give up the control of the airport, or was that still to be negotiated during the next day; the fact whether, and under what conditions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the last day of the negotiations started with little change in the -- in the Serb position, although they had indicated the night before that there might be some flexibility. Principally General Mladic was still saying he -- he wouldn't comply, would not hand over the airport. And it was a restatement of the Serb position that they would like to retain these control positions so it would allow them to retain effective control. I can't recall the exact words now, but at some point in time it was clear that Mr. Thornbury said to them, Look, if this is where -- where we are and we can't make any ground, then I have to pack up and go back to -- to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the core issue was still there to be settled on that final day; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The issue was the control of the airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did the Federation still insist on including the second stage, the demilitarisation to be dealt with at the same time, or --

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The Presidency, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Presidency, yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, they did. In fact, it was quite late in the day before Mr. Ganic and President Izetbegovic finally agreed and did so very reluctantly. It may have even been in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. Is there any need to put further questions to the witness, any issue triggered by questions of the Bench? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: None on behalf of the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, nor of the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wilson, this, then, concludes your evidence in this Court. I'd like to thank you for coming and having answered questions, both of the parties and of the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip. In your career saying "a safe trip home" might not -- where your home is might not always be that clear, but at least a safe trip wherever you go at this moment. You're excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, please escort Mr. Wilson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon it's clear that your next witness will not be called until tomorrow, as far as I understand. I inform the parties that we'll have a late start tomorrow in the afternoon due to scheduling problems. One of the Judges of this Bench has to attend a Status Conference. So we assume that we'll start at 3.30. But, of course, I cannot give a guarantee that it could not be a little bit later. I'd like to use the time. First of all, we have to deal with the exhibits in relation to Mr. Wilson. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits P720, P721, and P722. P720 and P722 still require B/C/S translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, when those are available to us, we will submit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't hear any objections until now. The Defence, of course, will have an opportunity to object as soon as the translations are there. P720 to 722 are admitted into evidence, provisionally to the extent that translations are still expected. Then I'd like to spend some time on procedural issues. First of all, is there any observation to be made by the parties, perhaps briefly at this moment, on the guidance the Chamber gave yesterday on how to deal with expert reports? Mr. Stewart, do you have any observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Only this, Your Honour: We -- we have, I confess, hadn't had an opportunity to gather on the Defence side to -- to consider it in any depth. We -- we should just say they are guidelines, we understand, that expressly any submissions as to particular material going in will be listened to and considered and so on. So on that basis, nothing is shut out if it actually does turn out to be of significance. And, Your Honour, we -- we certainly support the notion of not having absolutely hundreds and hundreds of documents and having them churned through hour by hour as we're in court. So, Your Honour, we don't really have any -- any further observations than that, on the basis that there's always that flexibility, and if the material is needed it -- it will go in. We don't have anything further to observe now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the main reason for suggesting this is that if the supporting material would not allow for the opinion and the conclusions drawn by the expert, that then they should be on our table and we should be able to identify any deficiencies in the way the expert worked. And at the same time, we want to avoid that just for -- as a matter of not missing one, to have 500 documents on our table because we are afraid that we might need one of the 500 at a later stage and therefore identify them in an early stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We understand that, Your Honour, and perhaps, as an example, if an expert says or assumes that a particular decision was minuted on a particular day and it is minuted and there isn't challenge as to the authenticity of the minute, then that may be that that piece is paper is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- just not worth Your Honours having. We understand that's an illustration of what Your Honours had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the conclusions of the expert are not supported by the material he claims that supports his conclusion, then we should look at that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also add to that that in our experience we have also seen that we get the minutes of a specific meeting, which is 100 or 120 pages, and we need only one or two pages of that meeting. So under those circumstances, if one of the parties would like to tender this relevant portion of that meeting, we could try to find a solution by saying, This is the cover page, this is the first page which says those and those are present, parties do agree that those present did not leave halfway or that not others came in. And then we concentrate on, well, let's say, the page -- the relevant page and perhaps the page prior to that and the page after that, but not necessarily have six times copied 120 pages where we actually are in need only of three, four, or five pages at the most. Mr. Harmon, I should have given you an opportunity first before I commented on what Mr. Stewart said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate being given the opportunity, Your Honour. I will say that at first blush this causes the Prosecution some concerns, and we are interested in reaching practical solutions. We appreciate the Court's views. The Court always takes a pragmatic approach to these issues. And we are interested in finding solutions that address our needs and the Court's needs. Let me give you an example of what concerns us: We have a limited amount of time in dealing with the experts in their testimony. Some experts four hours. But their expertise covers an area of subjects that is quite broad. There may be a number of documents, for example, in the expert's testimony or in the expert report that are not controversial, that are not in any way at all an issue but which are significant evidence for us. We want to be able to rely on that evidence that has not been exposed in the limited four hours or six hours of examination allotted to the Prosecutor's Office that is not controversial, and we don't want it excluded, for example, under the possibility, as articulated in the position -- in point number 5. So there's that concern for us. The expert reports rely on a significant number of footnotes. I was looking, for example, earlier today at Ewan Brown's expert report. It had, I think, 800-plus footnotes. Many of those footnotes had been already -- the documents contained in those footnotes have already been introduced elsewhere. In Patrick Treanor's expert report, for example, references to the Assembly session meetings. Those are already in evidence. Those are not going to be at issue in any -- or not going to be brought out necessarily or at great length in the testimony of Mr. Brown. However, in the final arguments, in the final trial brief, we want to be able to cite two documents that do support Mr. Brown's conclusions. And because we don't bring them out during the course of the examination, the four hours, for example, that we have with the expert, or because they are not in controversy, we fear the possibility of the evidence being excluded that we wouldn't necessarily address during our examination of the witness but that we may want to rely upon and cite to the Court during the final trial brief, during the final submissions to the Chamber. So that's what concerns us, the exclusionary aspect of this. I don't think the Court intends to be unduly restrictive. I think the Court will be open and flexible. And I want to reiterate that we're certainly more than willing to sit down with counsel to try to identify in expert reports what issues are in controversy so we can hone in on those. I will make that proposition to Mr. Stewart later. If we could somehow reach an agreement on how to identify those issues, we'll focus on those issues. But I think it's important for the Court to be able to have during its deliberations essentially the archive of material that's available to the expert to support certain positions. I may not in the course of the examination of the witness make accurate assessments as to what could be of interest to the Trial Chamber. It may well be that in deliberations the Trial Chamber says in its deliberations, Let's consider this particular point. What is there to support that point? I'd like to see what supports the expert's view on that. If during the course of the examination of the expert that hasn't been touched upon and if under point 5 that would be excluded, then it seems to me that the Court may potentially be handicapped in its deliberations on particular points that were not identified by the parties during the course of the examination of the expert. Therefore, our view -- our concerns, Your Honour - and as I say, we're willing to sit down and try to work this out in practical means - is that exclusion could be detrimental both to the parties and to the Court in its ultimate deliberations. I agree with the Court that a 170-page document that has two pages of relevant information is what's important to be considered by the Court, and we will take steps, and affirmative steps, to identify those materials so as to make the tasks of the parties and the Court sufficiently focussed on the issues and the matters that are at issue. Those are the views that we have and our -- and those are the principal concerns that we have about the proposal. We understand that it's only a proposal. My suggestion is that we consider this over the upcoming days and deal with those, try to work these matters out with the - - with the parties. I know, for example, that considerable work has already been done on structuring examinations of experts already that this report -- this proposal makes us go back to the beginning of that and try to take all these concerns in, and it is a Herculean task to try to restructure these testimonies in light of this proposal. Those are my remarks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first say one thing exactly, because we were confronted with a similar Herculean task, that we came with it at least not at the very -- at the eve before the experts would testify; therefore, we tried to come with it a bit more in advance. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, a lot of what Mr. Harmon says, in our submission, demonstrates what we respectfully suggest is the considerable sense of the guidelines indicated by the Trial Chamber. Mr. Harmon says, for example, that it may well be that in its deliberations the Trial Chamber says, Well, let's consider this particular point. What is there to support that point? I'd like to see what supports the expert's view on that. We -- we understand paragraph 5 of the Trial Chamber's guidelines to cover exactly that situation, among others. The Trial Chamber then requests that information, because it does come to the conclusion that there is a point there which really does require the supporting material to be produced on reflection and could therefore ask for it. So that's -- in a sense, that's -- that's not the biggest point. The biggest -- or the bigger issue is this: That when Mr. Harmon says that - and I'm paraphrasing here - he's really reluctant to have this material put on one side because the Prosecution may, then, want to refer to it in closing arguments. This is exactly the problem which, to some extent, the Trial Chamber but certainly the Defence faces - and perhaps the Prosecution would face it the other way round, although frankly the Defence's rather more limited resources do give us rather less opportunity - but Your Honours would have seen that we're faced sometimes with an overwhelming amount of material, and then the Prosecution makes a selection of items to actually bring forward for specific presentation to the Trial Chamber. And the coincidence between what the Prosecution actually brings up in the course of the witness's evidence and what might subsequently be relied upon as being important is not always completely clear. And what the Trial Chamber's guidelines would achieve is that the Prosecution then - and it will apply to us when it comes to our turn - but the Prosecution then will be brought to focus on the important items which it wishes to rely upon at the right stage, which is when the witness is giving his evidence. So the Defence, then, are put in a fair position to cross-examine on the specific focussed issues, and this stuff is not left on one side buried in a -- a mountain of -- of paper to be unearthed later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let one thing be clear: What the Chamber intends is to find out where exactly the conclusions or opinions of the expert ask for further exploration of the supporting factual material. Let Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. me just give you an example: If a witness would say, In all municipalities on from a certain moment bakeries were now called cafes in the future. And if in the footnote he gives six decisions of municipal organs, then if neither of the parties presents these documents, the Chamber on the basis of the expert opinion could take into account that on from that moment bakeries, at least in a number of municipalities, were called cafes. If, however, one of the parties would say, Well, these decisions say just the other way around, all cafes were now called bakeries for the future, then of course we would have to look to that. So, therefore, we want to identify when the witness appears what factual supporting material -- because experts are not always best qualified to establish underlying facts. It will very often be on the basis of documents. We'd like to know at that early stage where this material would need to be looked at in further detail before we could form an opinion on -- we could assess whether or not we could accept the expert opinion. And, of course, if you'd say, Mr. Harmon, at the very end you'd like to rely on that material, the whole exercises for trying to do that at an early stage -- and I can imagine that the parties would just say, Well, I might overlook one or two, so we'll give each other a margin of 10 or 20 sources that could be additionally - without, of course, any further comment - but to give 10 or 20 of these sources to be made available if need be. But we should take care that the remedy is not worse than the illness. And if the remedy is let's put everything in because we might miss one item, then the remedy has become worse. I suggest to the parties that we'll have a break of half an hour, that I'll then read a couple of decisions still pending, and that the Chamber waits until further talks between the parties may have resulted in suggestions on how to proceed further with the expert evidence. We'll adjourn until five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll deliver a couple of decisions on behalf of the Chamber. Prepare yourselves. There might be some five or six. The first is a decision on motions for admissions of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis in the cases of Witness Selak and Witness 665. This is a decision on two Prosecution motions regarding the evidence of two witnesses, Witness Selak and Witness 665. The first motion is the so-called sixth motion for admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis. One of the witnesses put forth in that motion is Osman Selak. He has now been incorporated in what we now call the fifth batch of 92 bis witnesses. The Chamber has now decided to treat this case separately from the witnesses in the fifth batch because we have been informed by the Prosecution that it would be possible to have Mr. Selak scheduled to testify in the near future, if the Chamber would decide to require him to be present. The Chamber has considered the Defence's remarks on Selak, as well as the Prosecution's reply. The Defence does not oppose admission on the condition that there is an opportunity for cross-examination. The Prosecution, as I have suggested already, does not object to cross- examination. The Chamber is of the opinion that Selak's evidence meets the 92 bis admissibility requirements, but it is not fully admissible without cross-examination. The Chamber will therefore admit the evidence, except for the Tadic transcripts, which I'll treat separately, and on the condition that Mr. Selak appears for cross-examination. As for the Tadic transcripts, the Chamber does not find them relevant. If the Prosecution -- and perhaps I should say that a bit more precisely. That major portions of it, such as the military booklet of Mr. Tadic, which has been dealt with extensively, we do not find that relevant, and the Prosecution has made no selection, as the Defence has clearly indicated. If the Prosecution would like to come back with a specific request about portions of the Tadic transcripts, the Chamber is willing to consider them. In preparation for the hearing of the witness, the Prosecution is requested to provide the Chamber with the exhibit marked P1582 in the Brdjanin case. Lastly, the Chamber requests the Prosecution, prior to handing the witness over for cross-examination, to examine the witness on the meaning of the sentence at page 13069 of the Brdjanin transcript, lines 5 to 7. I now turn to the motion concerning Witness 665. On the 22nd of April, 2005, the Prosecution requested the admission into evidence of certain excerpts of the witness's testimony in the Milosevic case, as well as around 200 pages of transcripts from the Brdjanin trial, along with certain exhibits. The Defence was late in responding. It first communicated its position on the 12th of May, explaining that the lead counsel had inadvertently overlooked the deadline. The Defence filed its formal submission on the 17th of May, together with a motion for acceptance of the late submission. The Chamber accepts the lead counsel's assurances that this was an exceptional oversight and has therefore considered the Defence's reply to the Prosecution's motion. The Chamber accepts the Defence's position that the two portions of the Brdjanin text, as identified by the Defence, are not appropriate for 92 bis admission and must therefore be redacted. This evidence is to be elicited orally by the Prosecution when the witness attends, if the Prosecution wishes to do so. The Chamber, however, does not agree with the Defence's further point that certain portions of the Milosevic text, as identified by the Defence, constitute submissions by counsel and therefore are not evidence. That text, in the Chamber's view, is admissible. In conclusion, the Chamber decides to allow the Prosecution's motion in relation to Witness 665, with the two exceptions mentioned above, and on the condition that the witness is called for cross-examination. This concludes the Chamber's decision on these two matters. I will now turn to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I just ask a question on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it -- on that last point -- I'm not in effect appealing the decision, but on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You wouldn't need anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. I understand. I'd appeal to somewhere else anyway. It's only, perhaps, for clarification. Is it that -- did I make a mistake somewhere in submitting that that material was not, in fact, part of the witness's testimony or -- or is the Trial Chamber saying that it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to say that the words that appear there are not words spoken by the witness, at least for the vast majority, then it certainly must have been a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I'll double-check that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless we made a mistake in reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is -- we all make mistakes, and I certainly am not immune from that process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But I'd really thought I had identified the witness as being part of the testimony but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness will be called for cross-examination anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd like to make any further submissions in that respect on the basis that you might have been mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly possible, Your Honour. It's happened before, and it will probably happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I now move to the decision on the Defence's application for further cross-examination of Witness Bjelobrk. For the sake of clarity, I will recall briefly the context in which this submission was made. On the 9th and the 10th of November, 2004, the Prosecution examined Mr. Bjelobrk for approximately three and a half hours using the 89(F) procedure. On the 11th of November, the Defence cross-examined the witness for approximately three hours. Before commencing its cross-examination, the Defence informed the Chamber that it had not had enough time to take full instructions from the accused and to fully prepare the cross-examination. At the end of the hearing on the same day, the Defence requested the Chamber to recall Mr. Bjelobrk for further cross-examination if the Prosecution did not agree to redact certain paragraphs of his statement. The Chamber reserved its decision in order for the parties to have an opportunity to discuss a possible redaction of the statement. On the 28th of February, 2005, the Prosecution submitted a redacted version of the statement to the Chamber and to the Registry, but at the same time indicated that some areas of disagreement between the parties remained. On April 6th, the Chamber declared that while it was not inclined to allow further cross-examination, it would wait to hear further from the Defence. On the 11th of April, the Defence made its submissions through the legal staff of the Chamber, arguing that Mr. Bjelobrk should be recalled mainly because there remained significant unredacted paragraphs of the witness statement on which the Defence had not had an opportunity to cross-examine. Moreover, counsel for the Defence had been asked by the accused to confront the witness with around 50 documents relating to crucial parts of the witness's statement. By e-mail dated the 13th of April, the Prosecution informed the Chamber that while it considered that the Defence had sufficiently cross- examined Mr. Bjelobrk, it was not opposed to the witness being recalled. The Chamber has taken note of the fact that the Prosecution is not willing further to redact the statement of the witness. The Chamber has reviewed the paragraphs in dispute among the parties and the extent to which the Defence has already cross-examined the witness on those paragraphs. On this basis, the Chamber finds that further cross- examination of Mr. Bjelobrk may assist with the determination of issues central to the case as well as with the assessment of the credibility of the witness. The Chamber therefore grants the request, but limits further cross-examination to a maximum of one hour and a half. The Defence is requested to submit to the Chamber all documents it intends to present to the witness three days prior to the scheduled date for the continuation of cross-examination. This concludes the Chamber's decision on the matter of Mr. Bjelobrk. The next decision is a decision on Defence motions to strike evidence from the record. This is a decision on two separate Defence motions to strike portions of the testimony of Witness 73 from the public record. One motion, made in court on the 18th of April, is a request to strike from the record that portion of Witness 73's testimony in which the witness asserted that the word - and I quote - "Momo", which came up in two intercepts, was a reference to Momcilo Krajisnik. The transcript references for that portion of testimony are pages 12250, line 2, to page 12269, line 17. The Defence based its submissions on the prejudicial nature of the evidence and its lack of probative value. It suggested that the evidence be struck from the record with the provision for it to be placed back on the record should corroborative evidence emerge. The Prosecution did not respond to the submissions of the Defence on probative value but suggested that the Chamber should reserve its ruling on the matter in the event that evidence going to corroborate Witness 73's assertion should emerge at a later stage. In a second motion, made in court on the 14th of April - perhaps I should call that the first motion - the other motion made in court on the 14th of April, the Defence requested that Witness 73's testimony on transcript pages 12127 to 12130, concerning the issuance of firearm permits over a ten-year period from 1981 to 1991, be struck from the record. The Defence submitted that as no reference was made to any particular year within that period and given that the SDS party was not formed until 1990, the evidence was entirely irrelevant to the issues before the Chamber. I will now briefly consider the law applying to motions of this kind. As the parties are aware of, there exists a distinction between the admissibility of evidence and the Chamber's assessment of the weight that should be given to that evidence. A decision to strike testimony from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the record amounts to a decision that the testimony is inadmissible. The standard for admissibility is found in Rule 89(C), which states that the Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. The combination of relevance and probative value means that, to be admissible, evidence must, on its face, have a tendency to advance the proof of a factual allegation which is in issue. On the other hand, in accordance with the opinion of Judge Shahabuddeen in the Musema Appeal Judgement, the Chamber considers that there is no requirement that evidence be shown to be reliable before it is admitted. Rather, the reliability of evidence is a factor which goes to the weight given to that evidence. Questions of weight are deferred to the end of the case when the Chamber can assess the credibility, reliability, and relevance of any one piece of evidence in light of all the evidence it received. I hasten to add to this that nothing in what I have said excludes a finding at the admissibility stage that evidence is inadmissible where it's so patently unreliable that it can have no probative value whatsoever. In applying the aforementioned legal principles to the first motion, the Chamber considers that the evidence in question cannot be considered entirely irrelevant to the determination of a factual allegation in issue in this case, nor is the evidence to patently unreliable that it is devoid of any probative value. The two specific points raised by the Defence, namely, Witness 73's credibility on this issue and his alleged failure to provide an adequate justification for his assertion regarding Mr. Krajisnik, are clearly matters going to the weight that the Chamber should give to this portion of Witness 73's testimony when it is assessed in light of all the evidence received. They do not go to admissibility as such. The Chamber considers that this motion can be distinguished from a previous decision of this Chamber to exclude a portion of the evidence of Witness Music under Rule 89(D), which provides that evidence may be excluded if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. In that case, the Defence was not in a position to cross-examine Mr. Music on the portion in question due to the very late disclosure by the Prosecution of evidence going to the core of the case and due to the Defence having insufficient time to consult with the accused about that evidence. The portion of Witness 73's evidence that is now in question arose from a question put to the witness by the Chamber. The Defence subsequently availed itself of the opportunity to fully cross-examine Witness 73 on his identification of "Momo" as Momcilo Krajisnik. In relation to the other motion we are dealing with here, the Chamber agrees with the Defence that evidence regarding firearms permits issued between 1981 and 1992 -- 1991, I should say, without further specific reference to any period within those ten years, is not likely to be of much assistance to the Chamber. However, the threshold for the admissibility of evidence is a low one. The indictment period covers the second half of 1991. Again, therefore, this is not a case in which the evidence concerned can be considered entirely irrelevant to the determination of a factual allegation in issue. The fact that the witness testified generally about permits issued over a ten-year period is a question going to the weight that the Chamber should give to the evidence at the end of the case. It does not render the evidence inadmissible. The Chamber wishes to remark that striking evidence from the record is an extreme measure which is not to be undertaken lightly. It was developed in the context of jury trials, where such measures may be necessary to prevent jurors from considering evidence that is unfairly prejudicial. In the present circumstances, however, there is no reason to believe that the accused will suffer prejudice if the relevant portions of Witness 73's testimony are allowed to remain on the record for the Chamber to evaluate in due course and in light of all the evidence. I do wish to emphasise again that mere admission of evidence gives no hint of the final weight, if any, that the Chamber will give to it. Both motions to strike evidence from the record are therefore denied. The parties are invited in future to consider such motions as a measure of last resort, to be invoked only when evidence is patently devoid of any relevance or probative value, or when admission of the evidence would impact negatively on the fairness of the trial. This concludes the Chamber's decision and also guidance on this matter. Before I proceed with the next one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now continue with the statement of the reasons for the oral grant of protective measures to Witness 101. On Monday, the 9th of May, the Chamber granted an oral request by the Prosecution to have Witness 101 testify in closed session. In its submission, the Prosecution observed that the witness was in a unique position in relation to a large-scale incident. The Prosecution submitted that the nature of the witness's evidence would therefore lead to his identification if he were to testify with protective measures less restrictive than closed session. The Prosecution also informed the Chamber that, after testifying with a pseudonym and face and voice distortion in another trial in this Tribunal, both the witness and a relative of his were subjected to threats of a serious nature. The witness twice received threatening telephone calls, including one directly related to his prior testimony at this Tribunal. On one occasion, a valuable asset belonging to the witness was stolen with an accompanying threat that if he came to collect it he would likely be killed. The Prosecution further informed the Chamber that the witness's family continues to reside in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Persons implicated by the witness in serious crimes continue to reside in the same area. The Defence did not oppose appropriate measures of confidentiality for a portion of Witness 101's evidence concerning the incident in question which the Prosecution proposed to tender under Rule 89(F). However, the Defence submitted that evidence concerning background events, which the Prosecution proposed to lead viva voce, would not lead to the witness's identification in and of itself. The Defence proposed that the Prosecution proceed with appropriate caution, leading this portion of Witness 101's evidence in open session, under pseudonym, with voice and facial distortion. The standard applied by this Chamber to requests for protective measures is by now very well settled. The party seeking protective measures must demonstrate the existence of an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family should it become known that the witness gave evidence. It's usually sufficient for a grant of protective measures if a party can show that a threat was made against the witness. The Chamber considers that the Prosecution established the existence of an objectively-grounded risk in the case of Witness 101. After an explanation by the Prosecution of the topics on which it proposed to lead viva voce evidence from Witness 101, the Chamber was also satisfied that measures less restrictive than closed session would not have dealt adequately with the legitimate security concerns of the witness. In the opinion of the Chamber, that evidence was likely to be of a sufficiently detailed and distinctive nature, particularly regarding alleged perpetrators of crimes and locations mentioned, to expose Witness 101 to a risk of identification should he testify in open session. This concludes the reasons for that decision. The next decision I will read is an order for the lifting of confidentiality on the testimony of Witnesses 73 and 239. This is a decision concerning the private- or closed-session testimony of two witnesses. On the 18th of April, 2005, the parties undertook to identify portions of the private-session testimony of Witness 73 which could be made public. Moreover, on the 20th of April, they undertook to do the same with respect to Witness 239. The parties forwarded the results of their discussions by e-mail to the Chamber. The Chamber has reviewed all of the portions of testimony identified by the parties in respect of the two witnesses and considers that they can be safely released to the public. The Chamber therefore orders the lifting of private-session confidentiality for the excerpts of Witness 239's testimony, as shown in a handout which will be distributed by Madam Registrar. I kindly ask Madam Registrar to file the handout when she has an opportunity to do so. In relation to Witness 73, the Chamber received a list identifying dozens of excerpts of private-session testimony that can be made public, as shown in that same handout just distributed. In the interest of giving effect to the agreement of the parties, the Chamber orders the lifting of private session for all those excerpts. However, with respect to future agreements on portions of private-session testimony that may be released to the public, the Chamber invites the parties to consider the value of releasing portions of transcript that amount to no more than a few lines concerning technical or procedural matters and which make no sense at all in isolation. A good example, or perhaps I should say an extremely bad example, of one such portion identified by the parties in respect of Witness 73 comes at page 12265 of the transcript. The parties have asked the Chamber to release to the public the following line. I quote: "Would there be any copies available? Yes." This concludes the Chamber's decision and guidance in this matter. I cannot resist to add to that that it seems that at least the one who proposed this - and I think it was from the Prosecution side - had more time available than was good for him or her at that time. That's just one example. I think the English Queen would have said that she would not be amused by it. Then I come now to the last decision I'll deliver today, and that's the order for the lifting of confidentiality on the testimony of Witness 60. On the 21st of March, 2005, the Chamber directed the Prosecution to review the private-session testimony of Witness 60 in order to identify excerpts which could be released to the public. This was done on the 23rd of March, and the Chamber issued its decision on the 27th of April at the last housekeeping session. At the same time, the Chamber invited the Defence to apply for further disclosure if it considered that other portions could be safely released to the public. The Defence made its application by e-mail dated the 6th of May, and the Prosecution responded on the same day. The Defence replied on the 7th of May. The parties are now in agreement that lines 11 to 19 on transcript page 10837 should be released to the public. The Chamber has reviewed the material and agrees that nothing in those lines identifies the witness. With respect to the portion of the text running from page 10871, line 9, to page 10873, line 1, the Chamber has reviewed the parties' submissions as well as the material. The Chamber is of the view that the text on transcript page 10872, line 21, beginning with - and I quote - "What I would like to know ..." and running to transcript page 10873, line 1, up to and including - I quote - "... young adult in that same village," can be safely released to the public. I note that this text is of little interest, since it does not contain any evidence. The Chamber therefore requests the Registry to release to the public the portions of the transcript identified above. This concludes the Chamber's decision on Witness 60's testimony. It's unnecessary to say that not the whole portion suggested was released to the public, but only part of it. This concludes this decision. We might find time tomorrow and the day after tomorrow to deal with a few other procedural matters as well, for example, thinking about the Brcko dossier. But for the day, we'll conclude. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, half past 3.00 in the afternoon in this same courtroom.
